definition: A discourse relation (also coherence relation or rhetorical relation) is a description of how two segments of discourse are logically and/or structurally connected to one another.
details: A widely upheld position is that in coherent discourse, every individual utterance is connected by a discourse relation with a context element, e.g., another segment that corresponds to one or more utterances. An alternative view is that discourse relations correspond to the sense (semantic meaning or pragmatic function) of discourse connectives (discourse markers, discourse cues, e.g., conjunctions, certain adverbs), so that every discourse connective elicits at least one discourse relation. Both views converge to some extent in that the same underlying inventory of discourse relations is assumed. There is no general agreement on the exact inventory of discourse relations, but current inventories are specific to theories or frameworks. With ISO/TS 24617-5 (Semantic annotation framework; Part 5: Discourse structure, SemAF-DS), a standard has been proposed, but it is not widely used in existing annotations or by tools. Yet another proposal to derive at a generalized discourse relation inventory is the cognitive approach to coherence relations (CCR) proposed by Ted Sanders and colleagues. This theory reduces discourse relations to a combination of five parameters. In addition to a discourse relation inventory, some (but not all) theories postulate structural constraints on discourse relations, and if paratactic (coordinate) or hypotactic (subordinate) relations are distinguished that hold across two or more text spans, coherence in discourse can be modelled as a tree (as in RST, see below) or over a tree (as in SDRT, see below).

explainer.lead: A discourse relation describes how one piece of text or speech connects to another, such as giving a reason, adding information, or expressing a contrast. These connections help explain why a sequence of utterances makes sense as a coherent whole rather than as unrelated sentences.

tiers.eli5: Think of sentences as beads and discourse relations as the string joining them. In “We stayed inside. It was raining,” the second sentence helps explain the first. Naming that connection shows how the two sentences work together.
tiers.practitioner: Discourse relations are used when annotating discourse structure and modelling coherence, with relation inventories chosen for a particular theory or framework. Some frameworks also impose structural constraints, allowing coherence to be represented as a tree, as in RST, or over a tree, as in SDRT. A key pitfall is treating one framework’s labels as universal or assuming the proposed ISO/TS 24617-5 standard is widely adopted.
tiers.paperLevel: For discourse segments a and b, a discourse relation DR(a, b) characterizes their logical and/or structural connection. One position requires every utterance in coherent discourse to be related to a context element; another derives relations from the semantic or pragmatic sense of discourse connectives. Inventories remain framework-specific, while the cognitive approach to coherence relations proposed by Ted Sanders and colleagues reduces relations to combinations of five parameters.

explainer.example: Consider “The match was cancelled. It started to rain heavily.” The second segment supplies a cause-like explanation for the first, so an annotator could mark a discourse relation between the two using the appropriate label in their framework.

usedIn.name: Discourse annotation
usedIn.detail: Annotators label connections between text spans according to a chosen relation inventory.

usedIn.name: Coherence modelling
usedIn.detail: Relations and structural constraints can represent how utterances form a coherent discourse.

usedIn.name: Semantic annotation frameworks
usedIn.detail: ISO/TS 24617-5, or SemAF-DS, proposes a standard for annotating discourse structure, though it is not widely used.

explainer.intuition: Readers understand more than the meanings of individual sentences: they also infer how those sentences fit together. A discourse relation makes that connection explicit.
howItWorks: Identify two discourse segments, such as individual utterances or larger text spans.
Determine the logical or structural connection between them.
Assign a relation from the inventory used by the selected theory or framework.
Where the framework supports it, combine relations into a constrained discourse structure.
explainer.whyItMatters: Discourse relations provide a way to describe and annotate coherence beyond sentence boundaries. They also give theories of discourse a structured account of how utterances connect.
misconceptions: There is no single universally agreed inventory of discourse relations.
A discourse relation is not simply a connective such as “but” or “because”; one view instead treats relations as corresponding to connectives’ meanings or functions.
Not every theory adds structural constraints or represents discourse as a tree.
